doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Records, KRE radio, Sinatra's autograph and Gene Krupa at Sweet's
summary: He learned of big bands from home records and Berkeley radio; recalls Harry James and Sinatra, and Krupa's Wire Brush Stomp.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: At that time? Not really. Not really. We had recordings at home — we had Paul Whiteman and Amos ‘n Andy and the Two Black Crows and a bunch of other names. We may have had something by Fletcher Henderson because we had records. See my dad, being a chauffeur, the people were always giving him records, the people he worked for. So we may have had Fletcher Henderson records. I know that I became aware of him — oh it was after my mother died. I became aware of him because we had a station in Berkeley called KRE and it was the equivalent of our KCSM here or the K-Jazz that we used to have. They would play jazz records. Big band records. Small group records. They had one segment was the Moldy Fig segment where they’d play all Lu Watters at the time and they’d play old Muggsy and they’d play the traditional New Orleans stuff. And then they had another segment where they would play Lunceford, Kirk, Basie, Duke, Louis Jordan, the Savoy Sultans, there was another guy — what the heck, they did the song called “Who Threw the”— Doc Wheeler. With “Who Threw the Whiskey in the Well.” Marvelous bands you know. And considering how crude the equipment was, gee, they were just marvelous. And the drums, of course you could hear the drums. I’d listen to those. But Fletcher Henderson, yeah. And when I really started getting hip to who he was I thought about how lucky I was, how I wish I’d been more on it, more hip, because I could have gotten their autographs. See when Harry James left Benny Goodman, in I guess the late thirties, he and Krupa both left, and they both played Sweet’s Ballroom. Harry James played Sweet’s and I went naturally, on the colored night, and there was the two singers you know. It wasn’t Helen Forrest, she was with Artie Shaw at that time, she was a brunette. But there was a singer. I don’t recall the name of the female singer, and there’s this male singer looking at the audience trying to make eye contact, a real thin skinny cat, blue eyes. And I got his autograph. It was Frank Sinatra. He had just put out “All or Nothing at All.” So there he is, just trying to make eye contact see? Because here was a whole colored crowd. And then Krupa, he came up here and he played at the bowling alley on Eddy and Jones Street. They promoted the public dancing there. But for

some reason or another it didn’t last as a ballroom so they eventually turned it into a skating rink and the eventually back to a bowling alley. But Krupa went over to Sweet’s. And he played Sweet’s Ballroom just that one night, I mean two nights, and on the third night I was there and he did that “Wire Brush Stomp” which was a famous recording that he did, and at the end of it he threw the brush out in the audience. Unfortunately I didn’t catch it. But he was another guy that was one of my idols.
